question: In 2021, an NFT of this meme's original 2010 photograph sold at auction for about $4 million, with some proceeds going to charities such as the Japanese Red Cross. Its canine subject, a female Shiba Inu, was rescued from a closing breeder around 2008 by a Japanese kindergarten teacher, narrowly avoiding being put down. That teacher's 2010 blog photo later inspired a joke cryptocurrency launched in December 2013 by Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer, which still uses the dog's face as its logo. Captions associated with this meme are written in broken English phrases like "such amaze" and "much wow," shown in multicolored Comic Sans font over photos of the dog. The dog behind it, often called the internet's most famous Shiba Inu, died in May 2024 at the age of eighteen after battling leukemia. For 10 points, name this internet meme depicting a smiling, side-eyeing dog.
answer: Doge [or Kabosu; do not accept or prompt on “Dogecoin”]

question: The music video for this song, posted to YouTube in August 2016 by a leopard-print-clad alter ego of Japanese comedian Kazuhito Kosaka, initially attracted little attention outside Japan. It went globally viral after Justin Bieber tweeted to his millions of followers that it was his favorite video on the internet, in late September 2016. At 45 seconds long, it became the shortest song ever to chart on the Billboard Hot 100, entering at number 77 and breaking a record set in 1964 by “Little Boxes”. Guinness World Records also recognized it for that same feat. Performed under the stage name Piko-Taro, for 10 points, name this novelty song whose title strings together a writing utensil and two fruits.

This character was designed by then-recent art school graduate Emi Nagashima, credited under the pen name “Amy”, after a droopy egg yolk she was cooking reminded her of unmotivated young people. It debuted through an in-house design contest at its company, Sanrio, in 2013. Officially described by Sanrio as loving soy sauce and being left alone, it is often drawn wrapped in a strip of bacon like a blanket. Its Japanese name blends a word for “listless” with a shortened form of the word for “egg”. In December 2022, it got a Netflix stop-motion series called “An Eggcellent Adventure”. For 10 points, name this perpetually exhausted egg-yolk mascot made by the Japanese company Sanrio.

This meme's feline-shaped GIF was doodled on a 70-by-70-pixel canvas by Dallas-based illustrator Chris Torres, who based its face on his real-life Russian Blue pet. It is soundtracked by a sped-up Japanese song originally written for the Vocaloid voice Hatsune Miku. The viral video, though, uses a cover sung with a different voice synthesizer named Momone Momo. Torres posted the animation to his personal website in April 2011 under the handle “prguitarman”; the character's body resembles a frosted breakfast pastry. It ranked among 2011's most-viewed YouTube videos worldwide, sharing the top ten with clips like “Friday” and a “Talking Twin Babies” video. In February 2021, Torres auctioned a remastered version of the animation as an NFT for roughly $580,000. For 10 points, name this meme depicting a Pop-Tart-bodied feline flying through space, leaving a rainbow trail.

Since the 1970s, some of these Japanese coin-operated fixtures have offered dual-temperature service, dispensing both hot and cold canned drinks from the same unit, marked with red and blue tags. Certain models can be unlocked to hand out their contents for free during earthquakes and other disasters. Despite falling from a peak of about 5.6 million units around 2000, Japan's roughly 3.9 million of these still add up to the highest number per capita of any country. Besides drinks, some dispense curiosities like canned bread, hot corn potage soup, or bananas restocked daily by Dole. For 10 points, name these Japanese street-corner fixtures that dispense drinks, snacks and other items for coins.

A 2012 revision to Japan's Animal Protection Law forced these businesses to close by 8 p.m., like other pet shops, until regulators granted an exception until 10 p.m. The concept was pioneered at a Taipei venue in 1998, six years before the first Japanese one opened in Osaka in 2004. Customers typically pay by the hour, historically around 1,000 yen, to relax with resident felines, appealing in cities like Tokyo, where strict housing rules make pet ownership difficult for many residents. America's first permanent example opened in Oakland, California, in October 2014. For 10 points, name this kind of establishment where patrons pay to spend time with resident felines.

This character and his giant robot were inducted into Marvel's mainline comic-book continuity through a 2014-15 crossover event that united heroes from many different parallel Earths. He gains his powers from the dying blood of an alien visitor, rather than a radioactive bug bite. To fight monsters that grow to giant size, he summons a 60-meter-tall robot named Leopardon, a format that Toei's Super Sentai franchise, the basis for the Power Rangers, would later borrow. Motorcycle racer Takuya Yamashiro played this hero across 41 episodes of a tokusatsu television series that aired from 1978 to 1979. For 10 points, name this 1970s Toei television adaptation of a wall-crawling Marvel superhero, notorious among Western fans for how wildly different it is from the American comics.

In 2005, a specially thickened variant of this product, nicknamed “Space Ram”, was developed with Japan's space agency for zero gravity. It flew aboard the space shuttle Discovery, letting astronaut Soichi Noguchi become the first person to eat one in orbit. Its inventor, Momofuku Ando, had earlier invented the world's first instant version of this dish, “Chicken Ramen”, in 1958, after World War Two food shortages inspired him to make an easy, shelf-stable meal. Its innovation was a container that served as packaging, cooking vessel and eating bowl all at once, with the food suspended partway up so boiling water could cook them evenly from below. It was launched by the company Nissin on September 18, 1971, and is now sold in more than 100 countries. For 10 points, name this global instant-meal brand, eaten straight from its own container after adding hot water.

Coin-operated capsule machines like these were first imported to Japan from the United States in 1965, before Japanese toy company Bandai entered the market and trademarked its own version in 1977. Its name comes from Japanese onomatopoeia: one syllable for the sound of cranking the machine's handle, and another for the capsule dropping into the tray. Mobile games that let players spend virtual currency on randomized characters or items borrowed both this term and its randomized mechanic. That practice faced scrutiny from Japan's Consumer Affairs Agency, which outlawed “complete” versions that resembled gambling in 2012. Prizes inside are sealed in small clear plastic capsules, ranging from character figures and keychains to novelty items and stickers. For 10 points, name these Japanese capsule-toy dispensers, whose name is also used for a randomized loot-box mechanic in many mobile games.

In 2014, this character's biography sparked a stir after Sanrio told a cultural anthropologist that despite her ears and whiskers, she is “not a cat” but a fully personified character. Her canonical backstory gives her an English birthplace near London and a pet feline of her own. Designer Yuko Yamaguchi has said she was drawn without a mouth so viewers could freely project their own emotions onto her blank face. She was first created in 1974 by illustrator Yuko Shimizu for the company Sanrio. For 10 points, name this bow-wearing icon whose face appears on everything from stationery to a Japan Airlines jet.
